extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of constitutional/political theory; legislators and reformers
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria and standards for assessing the design, composition, and functions of bicameral legislative chambers (especially a revising upper house and an elective lower house). Emphasises qualities a second chamber should have and the principal functions an elected lower chamber should perform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of State unity / local feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: A revising chamber (e.g., a federal senate or second House) should represent State unity and local feeling; this embodiment of local feeling gives the chamber respect and authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because each State feels that disrespect to the Senate is disrespect to itself, such a chamber commands respect and can act as an independent, efficient revising body. The local/state basis of representation is a foundational justification for a second chamber's authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence from constituencies and social bribe
rubrics_metrics.description: Members should have no constituency to fear and be 'accessible to no social bribe' so they can form disinterested, cool judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lack of electoral constituency and the social position of peers help make them less vulnerable to corruption; the chamber must avoid incentives that induce members to 'wheedle' or pander. The text notes the Lords are 'above corruption' in the sense they are the social influencers rather than the influenced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leisure to revise intellectually
rubrics_metrics.description: Members should have leisure and few distracting occupations so they can 'bury themselves in' the intellectual work of revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leisure allows peers to pursue politics undistractedly and to form considered judgments. This contrasts with those immersed in business who lack the time for close legislative revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate assembly and visible attendance
rubrics_metrics.description: A revising assembly must actually assemble and maintain visible, regular attendance; appearance of not assembling undermines legitimacy ('to look at it...in the ordinary transaction of business').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small numbers (e.g., 'perhaps ten peers', quorum of three) create an appearance of indifference. Apparent indifference is politically dangerous because 'the world must judge of you by what you seem.' Abolition of proxies and measures to increase actual attendance are recommended remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity of composition to avoid uniform bias
rubrics_metrics.description: A revising chamber should not be too uniformly composed (e.g., all landowners); uniformity causes it to guard only against a single error (excessive change) and biases revision according to one class's interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chamber should include a complemental critic who sees what the age misses. Without varied backgrounds the Lords' criticism is 'suspicious' rather than genuinely corrective; diversity of class and thought yields better revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit-based appointment / life peers
rubrics_metrics.description: Introducing life peers chosen for ability would supply the chamber with the critics and intellectual capacity it needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creation of life peers, judiciously and sparingly over time, would have added 'the very element which, as a criticising chamber, it needs so much'—able men from various departments (e.g., lawyers, literati, business leaders). Historical missed opportunities (Palmerston's proposal) are cited as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hereditary-only selection / recognition of average ability limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A hereditary chamber composed of eldest sons chosen by chance cannot be of above-average, consistently extraordinary ability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because membership is determined by birth and fortune, the average legislator from such a class will lack the breadth of experience and superior knowledge necessary to supplement the age's understanding; a miracle would be required for sustained superior legislative judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical business experience and knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Members should have real experience in business, trade, finance, and administration to revise contemporary statutes dealing with those subjects effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute book contains 'coarse matters' (trade, finance, statute-law reform) requiring practical knowledge. Young lords without administration experience are ill-placed to judge such matters; inclusion of business-trained men remedies this defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate role for aristocracy in diplomacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The aristocracy retains comparative advantage in diplomacy because ambassadors act as spectacles as well as agents and aristocrats are suited to that representational role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While aristocrats may be inferior in business administration, their social rank and experience of travel and high society suit them to represent the nation at foreign courts; this is an exception to general criticisms of aristocratic composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of judicial and legislative functions
rubrics_metrics.description: The judicial functions currently exercised (in practice) by the House of Lords ought to be separated: the supreme court should be a single conspicuous tribunal, not hidden beneath a legislative assembly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Having two supreme courts (Privy Council and House of Lords' committee) produced inconsistent decisions; the House of Lords is an accidental and ill-fitting judicial body, and the judicial prerogative should be reallocated to avoid competing apex courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent criticism of the executive
rubrics_metrics.description: The upper chamber should exercise a 'faculty of criticising the executive'—independent, impartial, clear, and supplemental criticism that an occupied minister might miss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should resemble figures like Lord Grey: impartial, clear, and able to take a supplemental or bystander's view. The chamber should host many such critics (life peers could help) to provide many-sided evaluation of administrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a leisured platform for Cabinet members
rubrics_metrics.description: The revising chamber should give members of the Cabinet who sit there a voice and 'position' enabling them to explain views with dignity and authority without being mere clerks of administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leisured ministers can speak with the force and dignity of rank; life peers increase the pool of such able, leisured contributors, improving the chamber as a political pulpit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against atrophy through neglect and class closure
rubrics_metrics.description: The real danger to a second chamber is inward decay—neglect, uniform class composition, and closed admission that shut out talent—leading to progressive loss of power and eventual atrophy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if safe from violent abolition, a chamber can lose influence if most members neglect duties, remain of a single class, and exclude genius without means. Reforms (life peers, end proxies) are preventive measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolition of proxies to ensure authentic attendance
rubrics_metrics.description: Permitting proxy voting enables non-attendance and undermines the appearance and reality of a 'real House'; proxies should be abolished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abolishing proxies would increase the attendance of considerate peers and prevent the 'whole House' from appearing a jest. Visible presence is important for legitimacy and effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dignity secondary to efficiency (House of Commons)
rubrics_metrics.description: The dignified or impressive aspect of a popular chamber is secondary to its efficient use; the House must produce real governing effects rather than merely impressive appearances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While institutions should have a certain stateliness to meet public imagination, the primary test is practical performance—how power is used to govern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electoral function: choose and dismiss the executive
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal function of the House of Commons is electoral: it elects and dismisses the executive (the government) and thus effectively chooses the nation's leaders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike an American electoral college, the Commons is a real choosing body with discretion; its maintenance or dismissal of a premier is the 'greatest duty' and a primary measure of its effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressive function: reflect the national mind
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commons must express the mind of the people on matters before it, making national opinions felt and offering an institutional channel for public sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By standing up for issues in the Commons, members can make the nation regard certain opinions as part of its intellectual sphere; this expressive role influences public recognition of grievances and ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching function: alter and educate the nation
rubrics_metrics.description: A great open council (Parliament) should 'alter' society for the better and teach the nation what it does not know; parliamentary debates should expand national understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parliament can introduce new ideas and make unfamiliar issues respectable and imaginable to the public; this educative role is a distinct civic function beyond legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informing function: lay grievances before the nation
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliament's modern informing function is to lay complaints and grievances before the nation (the present sovereign), making issues public and ensuring they are heard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This continues the medieval role of informing the sovereign; in a free nation the Commons ensures those grievances are placed before public attention, countering narrow private experience and biased press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative function is important but subordinate
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislation (making laws) is an important function but generally subordinate to the executive management of the state and to Parliament's political-educational roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While annual statutes and important laws matter (and sometimes must correct grave legal misfits), routine legislation is often technical and secondary to governance and national instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leadership quality: ministers must lead, not pander
rubrics_metrics.description: Ministers must lead the House decisively; a minister who 'succumbs to the House' or ostentatiously seeks its pleasure rarely succeeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A great deliberative assembly responds to worthy guidance; over-indulgence spoils an assembly. Firm leadership—directing rather than merely following the Commons—is a criterion of healthy parliamentary practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary success measured by maintaining government
rubrics_metrics.description: A practical test of parliamentary success is whether it maintains (or properly replaces) the government rather than the mere quantity of enacted measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newspapers may complain that 'Parliament has done nothing' if few laws passed; the author argues that sustaining effective executive leadership ('Parliament has maintained ME') is often the chief function and mark of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appearance and perceived legitimacy matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Appearances (e.g., attendance, visible engagement) often become political realities; a chamber that seems disengaged will be judged as such by the public and lose authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because 'the world must judge of you by what you seem,' maintaining visible activity and proper conduct is essential to preserve public belief in the chamber's usefulness.
